column4: In the same account of what led to the Fire, they say they were not among those who prayed; this makes the section's prayer abandoned by the heart part of a stated moral pattern, not a minor lapse.
The next confession is that they did not feed the needy, directly completing the preceding failure to pray and echoing the section's unnoticed absence of food for the poor.

The command “do not let your eyes pass beyond them” protects humble worshippers from being overlooked for worldly adornment; the verse also describes a heart heedless of remembrance, reversing the section's gaze toward brightness and heart gone from prayer.
The hypocrites rise to prayer lazily, perform for people, and remember God only a little; this closely joins the section's heartless prayer to its account of trying to be seen.
The same source-section root س ه و appears in سَاهُونَ: here the heedless are “in a cover” of heedlessness, giving the section's missed prayer a scene of being submerged from awareness.
The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” names the outward neglect that the section's dictionary gloss links to ي ت م: others fail to notice the orphan's right, unlike the commanded care.
This next rebuke says they do not urge one another to feed the needy, making explicit the food-shaped absence that the section sees in 107:3; 89:17 supplies the adjacent orphan rebuke.
The speaker recalls finding the Prophet an orphan and giving him refuge; the same ي ت م relation is answered here by shelter rather than the section's orphan-pushing.
The command “as for the orphan, do not oppress him” directly reverses the section's image of pushing the orphan and makes the orphan's treatment a test of response.
The adjoining command not to repel a petitioner extends the same refusal to push away a vulnerable person; 93:9 itself names the orphan.

The wall is repaired to preserve treasure for two orphans until maturity because their father was righteous; protection continues across paternal absence, reversing the orphan left without someone to keep him in view.
Those devoted to God give food they love to an orphan, a needy person, and a captive; the act directly answers the section's neglected orphan and unmentioned meal.
Their stated motive is God's face, with no wish for recompense or thanks; this contrasts the section's people trying to be seen, and explains the feeding in 76:8.
The difficult ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, giving a concrete opposite to the absent food and unurged care in the section.
The next verse specifies an orphan who is a near relative, applying the source-section root ي ت م to one of the people fed in 90:14.
The following verse names a needy person in misery, specifying whose hunger the food in 90:14 answers and completing the section's neglected-poor image.

Guardians test orphans until marriageable age and hand over their property only on finding sound judgment; the verse makes the source's “good comes late” dictionary gloss concrete as protection lasting until maturity.
The command not to approach an orphan's property except for its best use until maturity guards the child through the separation described by the source's ي ت م definition.
It likewise forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, turning attention toward a vulnerable right that can otherwise be missed.
Guardians must give orphans their property and not consume it with their own; this specifies a material form of the neglect and exploitation behind the source's account of withheld care.
Those who unjustly consume orphan property are said to consume fire; the sharp warning exposes the harm hidden by treating the orphan's property as available.
The verse warns against failing to deal justly with orphan girls under guardianship; it makes overlooked vulnerability a reason to limit the guardian's power.
It raises the rights of orphan girls whom guardians fail to give their due; this is a specific instance of the neglect attached to the source's orphan image.
Asked about orphans, the answer favors reforming their affairs and treats them as kin when lives are joined; this gives practical form to seeing rather than neglecting them.

When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an inheritance division, they are to receive provision and kind words; the scene puts overlooked dependents in view at the moment wealth is apportioned.

The needy may look rich because of restraint, while their marks let a careful observer recognize them; this gives the section's faint-star image a precise human counterpart: hidden need can be passed over by the casual eye.
The verse says that giving alms openly is good but giving them secretly to the poor is better; it distinguishes genuine care from the section's wish to shine before people.
It condemns spending wealth to be seen by people while disbelieving in God and the Last Day; this directly matches the section's account of people seeking visibility while neglecting real care.
A giver who spends to be seen by people loses the deed's fruit; the rain-washed bare rock makes display without lasting benefit a concrete reversal of the section's visible shine and missing aid.
The hypocrites “close their hands” and forget God, so He forgets them; the verse directly joins withheld help to reciprocal forgetting, as the section does.
The hypocrites urge others not to spend on those with God's Messenger; this is a concrete withholding of provision from a vulnerable group, parallel to the section's neglected food and small aid.
The instruction not to keep one's hand chained to one's neck warns against a closed-handed extreme; it makes the section's withholding of even small help legible as a failure of giving.

The source's dictionary gives س ه و a secondary sense of graciously overlooking another's slip; this verse commands pardon and overlooking, a deliberate, merciful kind of not noticing unlike neglect of the orphan or one's prayer.

This verse joins hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear with being heedless; it gives a bodily image for the section's eye missing the faint and heart absent from prayer.
People's accounting has drawn near while they turn away heedlessly; the source's gloss of neglect links this to the surah-wide denial of judgment that lets the orphan and prayer be disregarded.
The oath begins with the retreating stars; the next verse describes the runners that hide, making celestial withdrawal a specific parallel to the source's hard-to-see Suha.
The “running, hiding” heavenly bodies complete 81:15's retreating stars and parallel the source's faint star that disappears from an observer's notice.
The stars are dimmed in this end-time scene; it reverses the ordinary field of bright stars among which the source's faint Suha goes unnoticed.
The stars are blotted out at the Judgment; this cosmic loss of visibility sharpens the section's image of a small star already hard to see.
The “piercing star” is the conspicuous opposite of the tiny faint Suha in the source section, clarifying how brightness draws the eye.
The lamp's glass is likened to a brilliant star; this joins the section's star imagery to a striking, visible light, the opposite pole of the faint star overlooked among brighter ones.
The source's dictionary calls a rare single pearl “yetim”; here attendants are likened to a pearl kept hidden, making concealment compatible with preciousness.
The source's “single, rare pearl” dictionary sense meets the Qur'an's image of a hidden pearl: what is out of sight may still be precious, as with the overlooked orphan.
